title: One glucokinase, two tales of GLP-1 and insulin secretion
content: Glucose sensing in intestinal L cells has long been attributed to GK-catalyzed ATP production. A recent study in Vita revises this model, showing that glucose-bound GK closes KATP and triggers GLP-1 secretion without an ATP rise, separating nutrient sensing from metabolic permission and revealing how the same sensor is read in two distinct modes.Glucose is both a fundamental metabolic fuel and a major nutritional cue coordinating whole-body energy homeostasis. Following nutrient ingestion, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is released from enteroendocrine L cells to orchestrate postprandial metabolism through actions on pancreatic islets, the gastrointestinal tract, the nervous system, and other tissues [1–3]. For decades, glucose-triggered GLP-1 secretion in L cells has largely been viewed through the canonical framework of metabolic–electrical coupling. In this model, glucose enters the cell and is phosphorylated by glucokinase (GK), fueling glycolysis and mitochondrial oxidation. The resulting increase in the ATP/ADP ratio closes ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels, depolarizes the plasma membrane, and ultimately promotes Ca2+-dependent hormone exocytosis. This framework closely resembles the textbook model of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in pancreatic β cells [4–7]. Classic electrophysiological studies established KATP channels as a crucial bridge between glucose metabolism and β-cell electrical activity [4, 5], embedding a seemingly intuitive assumption into the field that GK acts primarily as a metabolic enzyme and that glucose must be metabolized before it can become a secretory signal.
